---
title: "Capstone project"
description: "Turn one of your own analyses into a pipeline that follows the lab template, then review it with a partner."
---

The workshops end here, and the real work starts. For the capstone you take
an analysis you actually run, as a set of scripts, a notebook, or commands
you keep in a text file, and turn it into a pipeline that someone else in
the lab could run on their laptop or on the cluster without asking you how.

You have three weeks. You work on your own pipeline and review a partner's.
At the end you should have something you will keep using.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you need before you start

- The two workshop days (modules 0-8), or the same material on your own.
- At least two of the [Snakemake-ify exercises](exercises/snakemakeify.qmd). Exercise 9
  (the whole `run_all.sh` as one Snakefile) is the best warm-up.
- A partner. Pair up at the end of day 2.
:::

## Pick a workflow

Use your own if you have one. Good candidates are things you run more than
once: a processing chain you redo for every new sequencing run, a QC report
you rebuild by hand, a figure you regenerate whenever the data change.

Keep the scope small enough to finish in three weeks. Five to ten rules is
about right. If your analysis is bigger, take the first half and stop at a
clean output (for example, filtered BAMs and bigWigs) that the second half
could pick up later.

If you have nothing of your own yet, pick one of these. Each one is an assay
the lab runs, and each is a chain of tools you have seen in the course or
can install from bioconda.

| Assay | Suggested scope | Things it makes you solve |
|---|---|---|
| CUT&Tag | Trim, align with bowtie2, filter, spike-in scaled bigWigs, peaks with SEACR, FRiP per sample | A second genome (the *E. coli* spike-in) aligned per sample; a scale factor computed in one rule and used by another; IgG as a control looked up by name |
| Micro-C | Start from the `.mcool` files MicroCPipe writes; insulation scores and pileups at a list of CTCF sites with cooltools | Inputs produced by another pipeline; a resolution sweep as a wildcard; one R or Python figure across samples |
| TT-seq | Start from TTpipe's BAMs; strand-specific coverage over a set of enhancers or eRNAs; a table per sample | Strand as a wildcard; an annotation file from config; an R script with `snakemake@input` |
| RNA-seq | Salmon index and quant, tximport and DESeq2 in R, a QC table | A contrast list in config; `directory()` outputs (Salmon writes a folder); one R step that needs every sample |

Do not rebuild MicroCPipe or TTpipe. Where a row above starts from their
output, treat that output as your raw data.

## The lab template

Your pipeline follows the same layout as the lab's pipelines. RegPipe, the
pipeline you built during the course, is the reference: copy its layout and
change the names. With `<Name>` standing for your pipeline's name:

```
<Name>/
  <Name>.sh                 launcher: reads the config, sources the profile, runs snakemake
  unlock.sh                 releases the lock after a crash
  <Name>Samplesheet.txt     one row per sample, tab-separated
  config/<Name>Config.yaml  every path, threshold and switch
  config/requirements.txt   Python packages for the launcher's venv
  profiles/local/           env.sh + config.yaml for a laptop
  profiles/<site>/          env.sh + config.yaml for a cluster
  envs/*.yml                one conda env per group of tools
  workflows/<Name>.snakefile
  workflows/rules/*.smk     common.smk plus one file per stage
  scripts/                  Python and R called with script:
  tests/test_dryrun.py      a dry run on a tiny samplesheet
```

Where to look while you build:

- RegPipe itself, in `course-pipeline/` in the course repository. Read
  `RegPipe.sh`, `workflows/rules/common.smk` and `tests/test_dryrun.py` first.
  The stopping points in `stopping-points/` show the same pipeline at earlier
  stages, if you want to grow yours the same way.
- The [field guide](field-guide/index.qmd), which walks through MicroCPipe,
  TTpipe and ChromSimPipe, and its [conventions page](field-guide/conventions.qmd),
  which lists the rules every lab pipeline keeps to (sample naming from
  `fileNamesFrom`, `outputDir`, where logs and benchmarks go, how profiles are picked).
- Module 3 ([config](lessons/03-config.qmd)) for the samplesheet and config,
  module 6 ([structure](lessons/06-structure.qmd)) for the layout, module 5
  ([cluster](lessons/05-cluster.qmd)) for profiles, and module 8
  ([testing](lessons/08-testing.qmd)) for the dry-run test.

## Deliverables

Tick these off in your repository's README as you go. Your partner checks
them in the final review.

- [ ] A git repository on GitHub with the layout above.
- [ ] `<Name>Samplesheet.txt` with the lab's columns, and sample names built from
      `fileNamesFrom`, not typed into the Snakefile.
- [ ] `config/<Name>Config.yaml`. No path, threshold or genome build hard-coded in a rule.
- [ ] `profiles/local/` and at least one cluster profile (`profiles/<site>/`, or
      `profiles/slurm-template/` filled in for the cluster you use).
- [ ] `<Name>.sh` that runs the whole pipeline with one command on a laptop and
      with `sbatch` on the cluster, and an `unlock.sh`.
- [ ] One `envs/*.yml` per tool group, with every rule that runs an external tool
      pointing at one.
- [ ] A `log:` on every rule that runs a tool, and a `benchmark:` on the slow ones,
      all under `outputDir`.
- [ ] `tests/test_dryrun.py` that runs `snakemake -n` on a small samplesheet and
      checks the job count, passing with `pytest`.
- [ ] One real run on real data (a subset is fine), with the outputs checked
      against your old scripts' outputs.
- [ ] A README: what it does, how to run it, what each output is, what you tested
      and on what.

## Rubric

Your partner and the instructor use the same table. "Meets" on every row is
a finished capstone. "Strong" is what a pipeline looks like when another
person can pick it up with no help.

| Criterion | Needs work | Meets | Strong |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Correctness** | Some outputs differ from the old scripts and nobody knows why | Outputs match the old scripts (same read counts, same peaks), or the differences are explained | Matches, and the README says how it was checked (commands and numbers from a real run) |
| **Reproducibility** | Depends on tools on your `PATH` or files outside the repository | Every tool comes from `envs/*.yml`; a fresh clone runs with the launcher | Versions pinned; a second person ran it from a fresh clone on another machine |
| **Configurability** | Paths or thresholds inside rules | Paths, thresholds and switches in config; samples in the samplesheet | Optional steps behind config switches; a new sample needs one samplesheet row and nothing else |
| **Readability** | One long Snakefile; rule names do not say what they do | Rules split by stage in `workflows/rules/`; clear rule and file names | A newcomer can find the rule that made any output file in under a minute; comments say why, not what |
| **Testing** | No test | `tests/test_dryrun.py` runs a dry run and checks the job count | The test also covers a switch (on and off) or a second samplesheet, and runs in under a minute |

## Milestones

### Week 1: plan and first rules

- Write down the old workflow as a list of steps, with the input and output
  files of each. This list becomes your rule list and your `rule all`.
- Set up the repository with the template layout (copy RegPipe and rename).
- Get the first two or three rules working on one sample with `snakemake -n`,
  then for real.
- Fill in the samplesheet and config for your test data.
- Meet your partner for 20 minutes: swap step lists and check each other's plan.

### Week 2: the whole chain

- All rules written, with logs, threads and conda envs.
- The full pipeline runs on your test data on a laptop with the local profile.
- Compare the outputs with your old scripts' outputs, the way the
  Snakemake-ify exercises do (`samtools view -c`, `wc -l`, `cmp`).
- Mid-point review with your partner (protocol below), on the dry run and the DAG.

### Week 3: cluster, test, review

- The cluster profile works: one run with `sbatch <Name>.sh`.
- `tests/test_dryrun.py` passes.
- README finished.
- Final review with your partner, then a short demo to the group: show the
  DAG, run the dry run, open one output.

## Review with a partner

Each review takes about 45 minutes. The author stays quiet for the first part
and only answers questions in the second.

**Before the review (author).** Push your latest code. Send your partner the
repository link and the one command that runs it.

**Part 1 (reviewer, 20 min, author watching).** Work through these on a fresh
clone, out loud:

1. Read the README only. Can you tell what goes in and what comes out?
2. Run the dry run with the launcher (`bash <Name>.sh -n`). Does it work
   without asking the author anything? How many jobs, and does that number make
   sense for the samplesheet?
3. Draw the DAG (`--dag | dot -Tpdf > dag.pdf`). Does its shape match the
   steps in the README?
4. Pick one output file and find the rule that makes it. Then find where each
   of that rule's settings comes from (config, samplesheet, or hard-coded).
5. In a copy of the samplesheet, duplicate one row and change its `Bio_Rep`
   (keep the same FASTQ). Dry run with that copy. Does the job count go up by
   what you expect? Do not run it for real.
6. Run the tests.

**Part 2 (both, 15 min).** The reviewer goes through the rubric row by row and
says which column fits and why. The author answers questions.

**Part 3 (reviewer, 10 min, after the meeting).** Open up to five GitHub
issues on the author's repository, one per problem, each with the command you
ran and what happened. Label the one you would fix first.

The author closes the issues before the next milestone.

## Getting help

Bring problems to your partner or the instructor with the command you ran,
the full error, and the rule it came from. Snakemake's error
messages name the rule and the file; paste those lines, not a screenshot.
